system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2124-04-08 13:14:00 to 2124-04-09 16:27:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with advanced HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, and a tracheostomy was admitted after a fall at his nursing home. He had lower abdominal pain and a positive urinalysis, leading to a diagnosis of a complicated urinary tract infection caused by Pseudomonas. He was initially treated with ceftriaxone, then switched to cefepime based on culture results. Imaging showed no acute trauma, and his chronic leg pain was unchanged. His abdominal pain improved with antibiotics. A midline was placed for IV antibiotic administration, and his foley catheter was exchanged. He remained stable, with no respiratory decline, and completed eight days of a ten-day cefepime course by discharge. He was discharged to extended care with plans to complete antibiotics and evaluate catheter necessity.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Other dependence on machines, supplemental oxygen
Pseudomonas infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site
Fall from other slipping, tripping, or stumbling

INDICATION:  ___ year old man removed GJ tube this am, inserted foley catheter
today to preserve tract, ?placement.  // ?placement

administration of contrast through percutaneous gastric tube.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal radiographs ___. CT torso ___.

FINDINGS:

After injection of contrast through percutaneous gastric tube there is
opacification of the stomach and proximal duodenum without evidence of leak.

IMPRESSION: 

Expected normal opacification of the stomach and proximal duodenum via
percutaneous gastrostomy tube.

INDICATION:  History: ___ with h/o of GJ tube removal, NPO at baseline for
aspiration.  // eval acute process, transmitted upper throughout.

TECHNIQUE:  Portable supine AP chest

COMPARISON:  Chest radiographs ___ through ___.

FINDINGS: 

Endotracheal tube is in place.

IMPRESSION: 

Tracheostomy tube is in place. The lungs are normally expanded with a
background of interstitial lung disease. There is no large pleural effusion or
pneumothorax. The costophrenic sulci excluded from view. There is likely mild
pulmonary edema. Heart size is normal. The mediastinal hilar contours are
stable.

NOTIFICATION:  Mild pulmonary edema on a background of chronic interstitial
lung disease. No evidence of pneumonia.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with dislodged GJ tube now with foley tube,
please place GJ tube.

COMPARISON:  Radiographs from ___ and GJ tube exchange from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS:  Dr. ___ resident, Dr. ___,
___ and Dr. ___ radiologist
performed the procedure. Dr. ___ supervised the trainee during
the key components of the procedure and has reviewed and agrees with the
trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
100 mcg of fentanyl and 0 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 70 min during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse.
MEDICATIONS: Fentanyl, lidocaine jelly.
CONTRAST: 45 ml of Optiray
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  30.4 min, 144 mGy

PROCEDURE:  Gastrojejunostomy exchange.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
health care proxy. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and
placed supine on the exam table.  A pre-procedure time-out was performed per
___ protocol. The tube site was prepped and draped in the usual sterile
fashion.

The existing Foley catheter tube was injected with contrast and showed
opacification of gastric rugae. The Foley catheter balloon was taken down, and
a stiff Glidewire was advanced into the stomach through the tubing. The tubing
was removed, and a short-term Kumpe catheter was advanced into the stomach
over the wire. Unsuccessful attempts were made to advance the wire and
catheter into a post pyloric position following exchange of the wire for a
___ wire. The short Kumpe catheter was removed, and a 6 ___ bright-tip
sheath was advanced over the wire into the stomach. A long Kumpe catheter was
then advanced through the sheath into the stomach. The stiff Glidewire was
then successfully passed through the pylorus and past the ligament of Treitz.
The catheter was advanced over the wire into the jejunum, and the stiff
Glidewire was exchanged for ___ wire. The sheath and catheter were then
removed, and a short catheter was used to measure the stoma length. The sheath
and long Kumpe catheter were subsequently advanced into their previous
position. The ___ wire was then exchanged for a stiff Glidewire. The
catheter and sheath were then removed, and a 18 ___ 3.5 cm stoma low
profile MIC gastrojejunostomy catheter was advanced over the wire into
position.

The catheter's balloon was inflated with 7 ml of contrast diluted in sterile
water in the stomach and locked in the stomach after confirming the position
of the catheter with a contrast injection. The catheter was then flushed,
capped and secured with sterile dressings.

The patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  Appropriately positioned new 18 ___ 3.5 cm stoma low-profile MIC
gastrojejunostomy tube.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful exchange of a gastrostomy tube for a new 18 ___ MIC
gastrojejunostomy tube. The tube is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. I see you came in because your GJ tube was pulled out this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I didn’t mean to. I was moving and it came out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve placed a temporary tube to keep the opening safe. It’s called a Foley catheter, and it’s in your stomach right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get my regular tube back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Interventional Radiology will replace your GJ tube tomorrow. It’s a quick procedure under imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I just want to get back to my meds and feeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you don’t miss anything. For now, you’re getting fluids through an IV, and we gave you a dose of metoprolol because your heart rate was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart? It’s been fast before…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. It’s likely from missing your morning dose and being a bit dehydrated. The IV fluids should help, and we’ll keep you on your usual metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I take a lot of meds… for HIV, seizures, breathing…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed all your medications. You’re on Truvada, darunavir, and ritonavir for HIV, Keppra for seizures, and your breathing meds like albuterol. We’ll continue all of them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach pain? It’s been off and on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your abdomen. It’s soft, no tenderness. We’ll keep you on hyoscyamine and cholestyramine for your chronic diarrhea and discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had loose stools again today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We won’t give extra constipation meds unless needed. Your body is adjusting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your lab results. Your white blood cell count was high when you arrived—17,000—but it’s already coming down to 13,000.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but you’re not running a fever or showing other signs. You have a long-term Foley catheter, which often causes bacteria in the urine without being a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. Your urine culture showed mixed bacteria, which means it’s likely contamination. We won’t treat it since you’re not symptomatic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows mild fluid in the lungs, but no pneumonia. It’s likely related to your chronic lung disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had COPD for years… and the trach helps, but I need suctioning a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re suctioning as needed and giving albuterol if you’re short of breath. Keep using the voice box when you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling? Any pain or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stomach feels okay. Still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. You’ll rest tonight, and tomorrow morning the GJ tube will be replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well last night. Your heart rate is down to 69, and your breathing is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Is it time for the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The radiology team replaced your GJ tube this morning under X-ray guidance. It’s in the right place and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No incision. They used a wire and a new tube over it. You were given light sedation and tolerated it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start my feeds and meds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start slow. The nurse will begin your medications through the tube, then your feeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We spoke with your sister and the nursing home. They said your Foley catheter was kept in place until you finished treatment for a past infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had it for over a year…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend removing it soon. It increases infection risk. You could use a condom catheter or urinal instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll talk to the nurse at the home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go back to the extended care facility today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back so soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your tube is fixed, your labs are improving, and you’re stable. Just keep up with your HIV meds, breathing treatments, and follow up with cardiology about your heart rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the metoprolol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking it twice a day. But talk to electrophysiology—they can decide if you need it long-term or an ablation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we reviewed your code status with your sister. She said you want full treatment if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I want everything done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. Your care team will respect that. You’ll be discharged in the next few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is ready. Remember to keep your GJ site clean, take all your meds, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’re here if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All right. Stay well, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Have a safe trip back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—discharge orders are complete. You’re officially discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. See you later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you made it to transport safely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Rest well.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with advanced HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, and a tracheostomy was admitted after accidentally dislodging his GJ tube at his nursing home. He was unable to take his morning medications and was found to have leukocytosis and tachycardia. He received IV fluids and a dose of metoprolol, which resolved his tachycardia. A temporary Foley catheter was placed to maintain the gastrostomy tract, and the GJ tube was successfully replaced the following day under fluoroscopic guidance. His leukocytosis improved without antibiotics, and urine culture showed mixed flora consistent with colonization rather than infection. He remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Chronic issues including HIV, seizures, COPD, and abdominal pain were managed with his home medications. The decision was made to remove his chronic indwelling Foley catheter as an outpatient due to infection risk. He was discharged back to extended care after a two-day stay.
